# Repositioning Strategy: From "Old" to "Original"

## A 30-Month Transition Plan to Recruit Under-35s Without Betraying the Base

---

## 0. How to Read This Document

Four things were asked for: **positioning**, **preserve/retire**, **channel and content**, **sequencing**. All four are here, plus the three things that determine whether they survive contact with the organisation: **governance** (which resolves the internal disagreement named in the brief), **measurement with a patience window**, and a **risk register with stop rules**.

The document is deliberately front-loaded on sequence and governance, because the brand's own history says that is where it failed — not on ambition or creative quality.

### 0.1 Assumptions, and the pre-work that gates the plan

This plan assumes a mass-market consumer brand with strong physical availability, a ~70-year history, an ageing loyalist skew, and two failed communications-led modernisation attempts. Five questions must be answered before money is committed, because the answers can redirect the strategy:

| # | Question to answer | Method | Time / indicative cost | What it gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Is the under-35 problem perception or availability?** Cohort decline is frequently structural — wrong pack sizes, wrong entry price, absent from convenience/quick-commerce/marketplaces, absent from the occasions the cohort has. | Demand-space / category-entry-point study; panel data decomposition (penetration vs. frequency vs. weight by cohort); channel share vs. category by cohort | 8–10 weeks; mid-five-figure to low-six-figure | Whether this is a distribution/format plan with a comms layer, or a positioning plan. If the brand is absent from the occasion, tone of voice cannot fix it. |
| 2 | **What are loyalists actually attached to?** | Qual with 20–30 heavy buyers; sensory/product-experience probing; CRM churn analysis | 4–6 weeks; low-five-figure | The Immutables list (§4) and the wording of the product commitment (§5.2) |
| 3 | **Which brand assets are distinctive?** Fame × uniqueness for name, wordmark, colour, shape, mascot, sonic cue, tagline, pack architecture — tested in *both* cohorts | Distinctive-asset grid survey, n≥1,000 per cohort | 4 weeks; low-five-figure | Preserve / evolve / retire decisions. Internal taste is not admissible evidence. |
| 4 | **Is the durability/consistency territory available and safe?** | Competitive claim-and-asset audit (§2.3) + category norms review + regulatory/nutritional/materials review | 6 weeks; low-five-figure | Whether we run Route A or a fallback route (§2.4) |
| 5 | **Can we survive transparency?** | Internal disclosure audit — sourcing, plants, offshoring history, prior reformulations, labour and environmental exposure, litigation | 8–12 weeks; legal + supply chain led | Whether the proof agenda leads with spec transparency or with something else (§5.1) |

**Total pre-work window: ~12 weeks, run in parallel.** No external activity before it completes. This is Phase 0 in §7.

### 0.2 The load-bearing insight

> Loyalists fear **product** change. Under-35s reject **borrowed** communication. Therefore: hold the product sacred and take the risk in behaviour, evidence and distribution — not in claims.
>
> **Change what the brand *does* before you change what it *says*.**

---

## 1. Diagnosis: Why the Previous Attempts Failed

| What was done | Why it backfired |
|---|---|
| Made "youth" the target and "modern" the message | Announced the brand's own insecurity. Effort read as evidence of irrelevance. |
| Borrowed cultural codes (slang, memes, aesthetics) the brand had no claim to | Unearned codes read as costume. The brand became a punchline for the audience it courted. |
| Implicitly repudiated the heritage ("not your dad's X") | Told the loyal base *they* were the problem. Repudiation — not change — is what alienates a base. |
| Led with advertising because it is fast and controllable | No product, pack, channel or service change sat behind the claim. Nothing was checkable, so nothing was believable. |
| Ran it as a "relaunch" — one big reveal | A reveal creates a single high-contrast before/after that critics and loyalists can both attack, and a single date the trade press can anchor to. |

**Conclusion: the failure mode was sequence and sincerity, not ambition.** The brand tried to persuade before earning the right to be heard, and tried to buy a new identity rather than reveal an existing one.

**A consequence we must plan for, not ignore:** both campaigns are archived, searchable and will be resurfaced the moment the brand appears in earned media. See §8.4 for the response posture.

---

## 2. The Strategic Bet

### 2.1 The reframe

**Do not modernise the brand. Reframe its age from liability into proof.**

Seventy years is not a nostalgia asset; it is a *credibility* asset — but only when expressed as evidence rather than sentiment. The bridge to under-35s is not "we're young too." It is a small set of values this cohort demonstrably rewards and that a 70-year-old brand can claim more legitimately than any challenger:

- **Durability over disposability.** The cohort most exposed to fast, cheap, short-lived goods is receptive to things that last.
- **Consistency as integrity.** "Not cheapened to hit a price point" is a strong claim in a shrinkflation era.
- **Verifiability.** Real factories, real people, real records — showable, not assertable.
- **Anti-hype confidence.** Quiet competence reads as high status; visible trying reads as low status.
- **Rediscovery.** A heritage brand can be *found* rather than pitched — a stronger cultural mechanism than being sold.

Critically, **each of these also flatters the loyal base.** They are not asked to accept a new brand; they are told their long-standing judgment was right. That is the mechanism that dissolves the trade-off between the two audiences.

### 2.2 Target definition (and why 25–34 leads, not exclusively)

| Tier | Who | Role | Investment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary growth: 25–34 "quality-seeking pragmatists"** | Entering higher earning years, burned by disposable purchases, value-literate, research-driven, marketing-allergic | Carry near-term penetration and margin recovery. They have budget, replacement occasions and a bias toward evidence — the shortest path from our proof assets to purchase. | ~60% of growth-directed spend |
| **Early funnel: 18–24** | Category entrants, platform-native, status-sensitive | Deliberately *not* the persuasion target, but must not be abandoned — if 18–24 never enter, we rebuild this plan in 2035. Presence, not pursuit. | ~15% of growth-directed spend, mostly organic/social/collab/campus/entry formats |
| **Retention: existing base** | Heavy, older, high-loyalty | Reframed as *proof*, not legacy. The most persuasive asset we own. | ~25%, weighted to CRM, product commitment, service, availability |

The 25–34 lead is a bet, stated as such: it is the cohort where our credible propositions (durability, verifiability, price integrity) map onto real purchase decisions rather than identity signalling. If the demand-space work (Q1, §0.1) shows the lost occasions sit predominantly with 18–24, weightings invert and the collaboration/format agenda moves forward in the sequence.

### 2.3 Competitive audit — before the positioning is locked

"The original / the benchmark" is contested territory. Before committing, audit:

1. **Heritage-adjacent challengers** already using craft, provenance and durability codes — often smaller, more credible and faster.
2. **Private label** using craft cues at a lower price, which can neutralise "quality" as a differentiator.
3. **Revivalist / archival brands** that own "original" more sharply than a continuously-trading incumbent.
4. **Own-category norms:** is heritage a positive or a penalty in this category's shopper language?

Output: a claim-availability map (available / contested / occupied) and an asset-collision check (are our colours, shapes, typography already coded to a competitor?). If "original" is occupied, we take the adjacent ground: *"the standard"*, *"still made here"*, *"the one that gets repaired, not replaced."*

### 2.4 Route branch: what if durability/consistency is unavailable?

The Route A bet (unchanged specification, durability) is powerful in tools, footwear, denim, appliances, cookware, spirits. It is weak or actively harmful where the category expects innovation (beauty, snacks, personal tech, trend-led apparel), or where "unchanged since 1955" translates as high sugar/salt, legacy materials or pre-modern ingredient standards.

| Route | Trigger | Where heritage credibility rests | Core claim shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Consistency / durability** *(default)* | Spec is genuinely stable, defensible and reputationally clean | Product itself | "Made to the same standard since 19XX." |
| **B. Institutional knowledge** | Category expects innovation; spec has changed | 70 years of accumulated expertise — we innovate from a deeper base than anyone | "Seventy years of getting this wrong before we got it right. Which is why the new one works." |
| **C. Provenance & people** | Spec unremarkable; supply chain clean and ownable | Place, plant, tenured makers, method | "Same place. Same people. Same method." |
| **D. Service & stewardship** | Product parity; aftercare ownable | Repair, guarantee, availability of parts, lifetime relationship | "We're still here for the ones we sold in 1998." |
| **E. Community & continuity** | Strong subculture or user base | The users, across generations | "Nobody's first. Everybody's last." |

Route selection is a gate, not a preference — decided at the end of Phase 0 on the evidence from Q4 and Q5 (§0.1). Routes B–E use the *same* architecture that follows: same governance, same sequence, same one-message rule. Only the proof assets and claim change.

---

## 3. The New Positioning (Route A shown)

### 3.1 Positioning statement

> For people tired of things that don't last and brands that don't mean it, **[Brand]** is the original **[category]** — built to the same specification since 19XX, because we've never cheapened it to hit a price.

*(Removed from the earlier draft: "the one the newest ones are copying." It is unprovable, defensive in tone, and violates the anti-hype principle the strategy depends on. If competitive teardown evidence ever substantiates imitation, let third parties say it — never the brand.)*

### 3.2 Components

| Element | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frame of reference** | From "the traditional option in [category]" → "the benchmark in [category]" |
| **Point of difference** | Uninterrupted standard. Dated, specified, verifiable. |
| **Reasons to believe** | (1) Published specification with unchanged-since date; (2) named facilities, tenured makers, documented process; (3) longevity evidence — durability data, guarantee terms, multi-decade users; (4) price-integrity record |
| **Internal brand idea** | **"Old enough to know better."** *Internal only.* It carries a parental register that would patronise under-35s if it leaked. Enforcement: it appears in the brand book and briefs, never in a deck shown to media/agency talent, never in creative. Consumer-facing equivalents are drawn from the alternates below. |
| **Consumer-facing lines for testing** | "Still Made Right." / "Nothing New Since 19XX." / "Proof, Not Promises." / "The Standard." |
| **Tone shift** | From warm, explanatory, reassuring → dry, specific, unhurried, confident; occasionally funny at its own expense, never at its customers'. Fewer adjectives, more numbers. Fewer promises, more receipts. |
| **Never say** | "New." "Reinvented." "For a new generation." "Not your parents' —." Anything that dates the *customer* rather than the *standard*. |

### 3.3 The one-message rule (primary anti-backlash mechanism)

Both audiences receive **the same substantive claim**, differentiated only by **channel, context and craft** — never by content.

Segmentation by media is invisible and safe. Segmentation by *claim* is what gets screenshotted side-by-side and destroys credibility. Operational test, applied at every asset approval: *could a 68-year-old loyalist and a 28-year-old prospect both see this without either feeling addressed at the other's expense?* If no, it does not ship.

---

## 4. Brand Asset Audit: Preserve / Evolve / Retire

**Governing principle: retire *behaviours and executions*, never *distinctive assets*.** Seventy years of memory structure is the brand's only unfair advantage. Modern-looking brands with weak mental availability lose to old-looking brands with strong mental availability.

### 4.1 PRESERVE — the Immutables (Tier 1: CEO + board sign-off to alter)

- Brand name and core wordmark structure
- Primary brand colour and its category ownership
- Hero product specification / formula / fit — **publicly committed as unchanged**, per §5.2
- Founding date and origin place as on-pack cues
- The signature sensory asset (pack shape, closure sound, texture, ritual) — whichever the asset test proves famous *and* unique
- The hero SKU's core price-value relationship
- The mascot/character *as a character*, where one exists and tests high

### 4.2 EVOLVE — same asset, contemporary craft (Tier 2: brand director sign-off)

| Asset | Direction |
|---|---|
| Logotype | **Redraw, don't redesign.** Spacing, weight, optical balance. It should look like a better *print* of the same logo. |
| Packaging | **Restore, don't restyle.** Strip accumulated 1990s–2010s clutter, sub-claims and starbursts; return to a hierarchy that lets founding-era assets breathe. The best design language is usually in the brand's own archive, not a trend deck. |
| Colour system | Keep the primary; build a disciplined secondary palette for range navigation. |
| Typography | Modern secondary type for digital legibility; heritage wordmark untouched. |
| Art direction | From staged and aspirational → documentary, material, close-up, process- and people-led. The factory, the hands, the wear, the 30-year-old unit still working. |
| Formats & pack architecture | Single-serve, trial sizes, multipacks, refills; formats fitting smaller households and mobile occasions (see pricing architecture, §6.2). |
| Materials & footprint | Refillability, repairability, recyclable substrates — framed as durability, not virtue. |
| Digital / CRM / DTC | From brochureware to useful: spec transparency, provenance lookup, repair and parts, subscription for consumables. |

### 4.3 RETIRE — quietly, by replacement (Tier 3: team-level, no announcement)

- Taglines older than a decade that no longer carry meaning — retired by *replacement over time*, never a farewell campaign
- The mascot's performance style and schtick — keep the character, retire the act
- Aspirational-family stock photography and lifestyle tropes
- "New and improved" and any claim implying previous versions were deficient
- Sponsorships and partnerships with no strategic fit — let them lapse, don't exit loudly
- Nostalgia-as-content: reunion ads, "remember when", anniversary sentimentality. Heritage functions as **evidence**, never as **feeling**.
- Any asset scoring low on both fame and uniqueness — that is cost, not equity

### 4.4 Resolving the contradiction: tail SKUs and range change

The earlier draft promised "additive, never subtractive" and then instructed delisting of sub-2% SKUs. That is incoherent, and dangerous: in heritage brands, tail SKUs are disproportionately where the loudest loyalists live. Corrected rule:

**The hero product and its experience are untouched. Range change is permitted, but only under the Discontinuation Protocol.**

| SKU type | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Hero SKU(s) | Immutable. No change to spec, size, price architecture or availability without Tier 1 sign-off. |
| Tail SKU, low volume, **low loyalist intensity** (no CRM concentration, no community mentions, no review defence) | Normal range…[truncated]
